     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "b15a8780-acd7-4dc0-92f3-b45db0dae5dd", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_3led2nXyjz9rBnkgEvYv1u", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     61	
     62	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     65	
     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     67	
     68	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     69	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     70	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     71	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     72

     94	## Other performance topics
     95	
     96	### Micro-bursting
     97	
     98	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.

     100	### Volume initialization after restore
     101	
     102	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized.      104	### Burst credits
     105	
     106	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.

     110	
     111	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     112	2.      5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     12	- After a size increase, the operating system must extend the partition and the file system. The agent gives the commands; the operator runs them.
     13	- Read the requirements page before proposing a change on an older instance, or on a volume with an MBR partition (2 TiB limit).
     14	
     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.

     21	
     22	## Quotas
     23	
     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.
     25	- Discover quota codes by name with `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`. Never hardcode quota codes.
     26	- Read defaults from the Amazon EBS quotas page. For example, the default for snapshots per Region is 100,000 and it is adjustable.
     27	- The io2 regional IOPS quota is separate from the per-volume maximum. A request within the per-volume maximum can still fail on the regional quota. Existing io2 volumes already consume part of that quota.
     28	- Adjustable quotas are raised through Service Quotas. Quotas that are not adjustable need an AWS Support case.
     29	
     30	## Snapshots
     31	
     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.

     36	- Target tags for Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies are case sensitive.
     37	- Recycle Bin rules decide whether a deleted snapshot can be recovered. With no matching rule, deletion is permanent.

     2	
     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action.
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.
     17	
     18	1. Is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?
     19	   - Yes: **Instance**. Say "the volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type". If a volume is also flat at its own limit, report both and fix the instance first, because volume changes cannot deliver above the instance ceiling.
     20	2. Is the instance healthy and one volume flat at its own provisioned limit on the dimension its type is judged by?
     21	   - Yes: **Volume**.
     22	3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume's `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?
     23	   - Yes: **Burst credits**.
     24	4. Did an operation fail on a quota (error text names a limit)?
     25	   - Yes: **Quota**. Use the Capacity and quota headroom section of [review-operational.md](review-operational.md).
     26	5. Are all layers below their limits, latency at the volume's normal level, and queue length low?
     27	   - Yes: **Not EBS**. Check CPU, memory, network and the application.
     28	6. Are all layers below their limits but latency and `VolumeQueueLength` up while IOPS and throughput collapse? This pattern alone does not prove an AWS-side impairment. Check for a direct signal:
     29	   - `VolumeStalledIOCheck` failed (value 1) for the volume, or
     30	   - `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a status check as failed, or
     31	   - an open AWS Health event for the volume, its Availability Zone or its Region.
     32	
     33	   Then decide:
     34	   - A running AWS FIS experiment targets the volume or instance: the latency is injected. Say so plainly; it ends with the experiment (see Step 5 of [troubleshoot-performance.md](troubleshoot-performance.md)). Never recommend more provisioning.
     35	   - One or more direct signals: **AWS-side impairment**. Never recommend more provisioning. Follow the escalation rules below.
     36	   - No direct signal and no FIS experiment: **Indeterminate**. Keep the cause open. Do not name AWS-side impairment and do not recommend more provisioning. Tell the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard for an ongoing AWS-side issue and to watch the volume status checks and `VolumeStalledIOCheck`. If the symptom persists, follow the escalation rules below.
     37	
     38	### Qualitative attribution matrix for "is it storage?"
     39	
     40	From the attribution draft, with the numeric CPU bands removed because no public source states them.
     41	
     42	| CPU | Volume latency | Queue length | Likely attribution |
     43	|---|---|---|---|
     44	| High | High | High | Application drives heavy I/O. Both compute and storage are stressed |
     45	| High | Normal | Low | Compute, not storage |
     46	| Low | High | High | Storage. The application waits on I/O. Go to the decision tree |
     47	| Low | Normal | Low | Neither. Check network, locks and the application |
     48	
     49	"High" and "normal" mean compared with the same resource's own history and the type's documented expectation in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     50	
     51	## Escalation (shared capability)
     52	
     53	Escalate to AWS Support when either is true:
     54	
     55	- Scope signals: an open AWS Health event for the volume, Availability Zone or Region; several resources failing the same way; `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a failing status check.
     56	- A bounded investigation cannot explain the symptom: all layers below limits, no running AWS FIS experiment, no recent change, and the symptom persists.
     57	
     58	Specific cases:
     59	
     60	- Attach or detach stuck: the attachment stays in `attaching` or `detaching` and does not progress. Diagnose (instance state, device name, whether the volume is still mounted, any forced detach already tried), then contact AWS Support.
     61	- Modification in `optimizing` with `Progress` not increasing across several reads, or still optimizing after 24 hours. Tell the user the Amazon EBS User Guide says some performance changes take more than 24 hours, so this is a check, not a fault finding. Escalate with the evidence.
     62	- Snapshot stuck in `pending` with no progress change over the same kind of window.
     63	
     64	Evidence pack to include:
     65	
     66	1. Account placeholder, Region, volume IDs, instance IDs, snapshot IDs as read from the APIs
     67	2. The time window (first ALARM time, symptom start)
     68	3. Metric evidence with units (IOPS, MiB/s, latency, queue length, `EBSIOBalance%`, `BurstBalance`)
     69	4. Volume status and AWS Health results
     70	5. The latest `DescribeVolumesModifications` record per volume, and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events if that optional lookup was available
     71	6. What was ruled out and how
     72	7. The Gaps list
     73	
     74	## Review ratings
     75	
     76	Each review finding has:
     77	
     78	| Field | Values |
     79	|---|---|
     80	| Severity | `High`, `Medium`, `Low`, or `Indeterminate` (the data could not be read) |
     81	| Evidence | The values and API that show it |
     82	| Fix | A specific change with parameters |
     83	| Mutating? | Yes or No. Yes means the fix is a proposal for a directed action |
     84

The Summary table is required, not optional, and it comes before any per-area detail. Keep the six areas and the `High` / `Medium` / `Low` / `Indeterminate` scheme as written; do not invent new areas or ratings.

## Root cause
The bottleneck is the volume's provisioned IOPS. Instance i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) and throughput are not limiting anything. io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS) was idle until about 16:13 UTC. Then a write workload of small 8 KiB I/Os started and pushed the volume to exactly 1,000 IOPS from 16:20 to 16:44 UTC, which is its provisioned limit. Requests the volume can't serve right away wait in its queue, so VolumeQueueLength climbed from 0 to about 1.33 and set off the alarm. Write latency rose to about 1.33 ms per operation. That matches the queue length at 1,000 IOPS, so the delay is waiting in the queue, not slow storage. The other limits have plenty of room. Throughput is only about 7.8 MiB/s, far below the volume's throughput limit. The instance-level EBS limit checks (InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck) stayed at 0. The instance's EBSIOBalance% (its EBS burst allowance) held at 99%. Nothing changed on the volume: it has never been modified, so this is new load hitting a fixed limit, not a configuration change. What to change: raise the volume's provisioned IOPS with ModifyVolume (online, no detach). Size the new value to the app's real peak, plus headroom. A 10 GiB io2 volume can be provisioned up to 5,000 IOPS (500 IOPS per GiB). If you need more than that, also grow the volume, for example to 20 GiB for up to 10,000 IOPS. Alternatively, cut the I/O count by batching the 8 KiB writes into larger ones. Leave the instance type alone for now: c6i.xlarge has a baseline of about 10,000 EBS IOPS and is nowhere near it. Recheck it only if you provision near that number across all of its volumes.
## Evidence
- ec2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 as /dev/sdf.
- AWS/EBS (VolumeReadOps+VolumeWriteOps)/300s: 0 from 15:30 to 16:10 UTC, then 999.99–1000.05 IOPS in each 5-minute period from 16:20 to 16:40 UTC. That is exactly the provisioned 1,000 IOPS, a flat ceiling.
- AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength (average): 0.0 before 16:15, 0.20 at 16:15, steady about 1.33–1.34 from 16:20 to 16:45 UTC (the alarm).
- AWS/EBS VolumeTotalWriteTime/VolumeWriteOps: about 1.33 ms per write from 16:15 to 16:45. That equals the queue length divided by 1,000 IOPS, so the latency is time spent waiting in the queue.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes/VolumeWriteOps = 8 KiB per write. Throughput is about 7.8 MiB/s, far below the volume's throughput limit, so throughput is not the bottleneck.
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck = 0 and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck = 0 for every period from 15:30 to 16:45. EBSIOBalance% minimum = 99% throughout, so the instance's EBS limits are not the bottleneck.
- ec2 describe_volumes_modifications: no modification has ever been made to the volume, so no configuration change triggered this.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 1000 IOPS, 10 GiB)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge)
## Gaps
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no data. The IOPS ceiling was inferred from IOPS sitting flat at the provisioned value plus the rising queue.
- I did not identify the process or application on the instance that started the write workload at about 16:13 UTC, or whether its demand is above 1,000 IOPS. Size the new IOPS value from the app's own metrics or OS-level iostat.
- The other volumes on the instance (vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, vol-1234567890abcdef0_15, vol-1234567890abcdef0_19) were not checked one by one. The instance-level EBS limit checks show their combined load is not limiting.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

I'm confirming the io2 VolumeIOPSExceededCheck metric shows 1 from 16:15-16:45 and 0 before, a direct signal the volume hit its IOPS ceiling.

Instance-level checks stay at 0, with throughput running at 89% of baseline and IOPS well under the 6,000 cap — pointing the root cause squarely at the volume layer. The io2 volume sits pinned at 1,000 IOPS with VolumeIOPSExceededCheck=1, 8 KiB writes, and write latency of 1.33 ms versus the documented <0.5 ms for io2 BX, though throughput itself has plenty of headroom at that IOPS level.

What's unclear is why demand suddenly spiked at 16:19 after sitting idle — CloudTrail shows no write events or volume modifications in the last 24 hours, so this isn't a config change but an unidentified process or workload that kicked off then, which is still a gap in my investigation.

Now I'm sizing the right recommendation: the fast agent's numbers for io2 IOPS-per-GiB and instance baseline IOPS are both wrong, so I'm recalculating actual io2 max IOPS for a 10 GiB volume, the true instance baseline throughput, and how much headroom remains once I subtract the other volumes' current usage — and it's coming out uncomfortably tight, close to 99.7% of baseline once converted to IOPS at 8 KiB per I/O.

Given the low queue depth (~1.33) and 1000 capped IOPS, I'm reasoning through whether this reflects closed-loop demand via Little's law, suggesting uncapped demand could plausibly be in the 2,000–3,000 IOPS range, though this is speculative. Based on this I'm landing on a recommendation to modify the io2 volume's IOPS from 1000 to 3000 while keeping the 10 GiB size unchanged, staying within the volume's max ratio.

Working through the math, instance baseline throughput minus what other volumes consume leaves about 24 MiB/s headroom, which translates to roughly 3,000 IOPS at 8 KiB I/O size — confirming the 3,000 target is reasonable and stays under both the IOPS-per-GiB cap and the io2 throughput limit at that IOPS level. I'm flagging that pushing beyond ~3,000 IOPS would make the instance's own EBS throughput baseline the binding constraint, burning through burst balance, unless the instance type has higher baseline throughput — which I'd need to verify via DescribeInstanceTypes rather than guess from memory.

I want to quickly check c6i.2xlarge's actual baseline to have exact numbers, note that io2 IOPS pricing is tiered and will increase cost, and plan a rollback via ModifyVolume back to 1000 IOPS after testing (mindful of the 4-modifications-per-24h limit). I'm also discarding several incorrect claims from the other agent — wrong IOPS-per-GiB ratio, wrong baseline throughput figure, and the false assumption that other volumes weren't already near their throughput limit — before finalizing this as a Limits-category mitigation.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeQueueLength above threshold on io2 volume
**Description:** Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length ([redacted ARN]) went to ALARM at 2026-11-23T16:23:04Z. Average VolumeQueueLength was 1.335, 1.333 and 1.333 for 16:20–16:22 against a threshold of 1.0 (60s period, 3 of 3 datapoints). The volume is vol-0123456789abcdef0. The alarm is a test alarm with no actions.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:20:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Write workload saturating the provisioned 1000 IOPS
**Description:** A write-only workload (~8 KiB I/Os) that started at ~16:19 UTC runs at exactly the provisioned 1000 IOPS of io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0. Requests queue at the cap: queue length is ~1.33 and latency ~1.33 ms. The volume is healthy and the instance has ample EBS headroom, so the limit is the volume's provisioned IOPS.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **Volume pinned at its provisioned 1000 IOPS:** From 16:20 UTC, vol-0123456789abcdef0 has run at a steady 999.7–1000.3 IOPS. All of it is writes (reads ~0). That exactly matches the provisioned 1000 IOPS. VolumeThroughputPercentage is 100%, and idle time fell from 100% before 16:19 to ~0%. Throughput is ~7.81 MiB/s, which means ~8 KiB writes, far below any throughput limit. VolumeQueueLength (~1.33) matches the average write latency (~1.33 ms), consistent with Little's law at 1000 IOPS. Before 16:19 the volume was fully idle.
- **Volume healthy: no stalled I/O, status ok:** describe_volume_status reports ok for all 4 attached volumes, with io-enabled passed and io-performance normal. VolumeStalledIOCheck for vol-0123456789abcdef0 on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 was 0 throughout 15:50–16:48. This rules out a degraded or impaired volume. describe_volumes_modifications errored because the root volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 has no modification history, so no recent modification was seen.
- **Instance has IOPS headroom but little throughput headroom:** The c6i.xlarge EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (149.0 MiB/s). All four volumes together use ~1,502 IOPS and ~132.9 MiB/s. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%, and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck / InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0. With the gp3 co-tenant at ~125 MiB/s, only ~23.9 MiB/s is left, which is ~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB. That caps how far raising the io2 volume's IOPS can help. c6i.2xlarge would give 12,000 IOPS and 312.5 MB/s.

#### Gaps
- **Bursts shorter than a minute not visible:** Only 1-minute CloudWatch data was available, so bursts shorter than a minute can't be ruled out.

### Root Cause: io2 volume provisioned at only 1,000 IOPS for a new 8 KiB write workload
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS; [redacted ARN]) was idle until ~16:19 UTC. A write-only 8 KiB workload then started and needs more than the 1,000 IOPS provisioned. The volume has never been modified and CloudTrail shows no changes to it in the last 24h, so this is new load hitting a fixed limit. The binding layer is the volume's provisioned IOPS. Fix: raise it to ~3,000 IOPS with ModifyVolume.
**Cascades to:** finding-iops-saturation

#### Supporting Observations
- **Volume and instance configuration:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-a-io2) is a 10 GiB io2 volume provisioned at 1000 IOPS, unencrypted, attached as /dev/sdf. Instance i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (example-perf) is a running c6i.xlarge in us-east-1a, launched 2026-11-23 07:56 UTC; describe_instances reports EbsOptimized=false. Three other volumes are attached: the gp3 root vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 (8 GiB), gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 (20 GiB, 3000 IOPS/125 MiB/s) and gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 (200 GiB, 3000 IOPS/125 MiB/s). The describe_volume_status call failed because it used an invalid filter.
- **Volume pinned at its provisioned 1000 IOPS:** From 16:20 UTC, vol-0123456789abcdef0 has run at a steady 999.7–1000.3 IOPS. All of it is writes (reads ~0). That exactly matches the provisioned 1000 IOPS. VolumeThroughputPercentage is 100%, and idle time fell from 100% before 16:19 to ~0%. Throughput is ~7.81 MiB/s, which means ~8 KiB writes, far below any throughput limit. VolumeQueueLength (~1.33) matches the average write latency (~1.33 ms), consistent with Little's law at 1000 IOPS. Before 16:19 the volume was fully idle.
- **VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1; instance limits not exceeded:** For vol-0123456789abcdef0, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck was 1 in every 5-min period from 16:15 to 16:45 UTC (0 before), meaning demand is above the provisioned IOPS. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck stayed 0. For gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 1 over the same window. InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed 0. Total instance EBS throughput is ~133 MiB/s, below the 156.25 MB/s baseline.

#### Gaps
- **The application's real IOPS demand is unknown:** The 1,000 IOPS limit hides how much the application actually wants. Check with iostat on the instance or the application's own metrics, then adjust the 3,000 IOPS target.
- **Process behind the write load not identified:** The process that started the 8 KiB write load at ~16:19 UTC on i-1234567890abcdef0_3 was not identified.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1000 to 3000 with an online Elastic Volumes change, sized to fit the c6i.xlarge instance EBS baseline.

## Reasoning
The volume has been held at its provisioned 1,000 IOPS since ~16:20 UTC (8 KiB writes, ~7.81 MiB/s, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck=1), giving queue length ~1.33 and write latency ~1.33 ms. It is healthy, so this is a capacity limit, not a fault. The instance EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS / 149.0 MiB/s; the gp3 co-tenant vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 uses ~125.07 MiB/s, leaving ~23.9 MiB/s, room for ~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB. 3000 IOPS triples capacity and keeps total instance demand under baseline (~3,500 IOPS, ~148.5 MiB/s). The change is online, with no detach or reboot.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current config (io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, in-use on /dev/sdf)…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State,Instance:Attachments[0].InstanceId,Device:Attachments[0].Device}' --output table
```
**Purpose:** Record the current config (io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, in-use on /dev/sdf) for rollback
**Advisory:** Make sure the saved values belong to vol-0123456789abcdef0 and not another volume on the instance.

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm no modification is in progress (NotFound or completed means…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Confirm no modification is in progress (NotFound or completed means proceed; modifying/optimizing means wait)
**Advisory:** This API returns only the latest modification; use CloudTrail ModifyVolume events to count modifications in the last 24h (limit 4 per volume).

#### 2.2 Confirm instance EBS throughput is still ~133 MiB/s (below ~135) before…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-data --region us-east-1 --start-time $(date -u -d '-15 min' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) --metric-data-queries '[{"Id":"rb","MetricStat":{"Metric":{"Namespace":"AWS/EC2","MetricName":"EBSReadBytes","Dimensions":[{"Name":"InstanceId","Value":"i-1234567890abcdef0_3"}]},"Period":60,"Stat":"Sum"},"ReturnData":false},{"Id":"wb","MetricStat":{"Metric":{"Namespace":"AWS/EC2","MetricName":"EBSWriteBytes","Dimensions":[{"Name":"InstanceId","Value":"i-1234567890abcdef0_3"}]},"Period":60,"Stat":"Sum"},"ReturnData":false},{"Id":"mibps","Expression":"(rb+wb)/60/1048576","ReturnData":true}]'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm instance EBS throughput is still ~133 MiB/s (below ~135) before applying 3000 IOPS
**Advisory:** If the gp3 co-tenant's usage has grown, pick a lower IOPS target.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Raise the io2 volume from 1000 to 3000 IOPS online
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000
```
**Purpose:** Raise the io2 volume from 1000 to 3000 IOPS online
**Risks:** Cost increase: 2,000 more provisioned IOPS billed per IOPS-month., Uses 1 of the 4 Elastic Volumes modifications allowed per volume in a rolling 24h; a rollback uses another.
**Advisory:** Real demand is hidden by the 1000 IOPS cap. Above ~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB, the c6i.xlarge EBS throughput baseline (149.0 MiB/s) becomes the limit.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Verify the modification reaches optimizing or completed with…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'
```
**Purpose:** Verify the modification reaches optimizing or completed with TargetIops=3000

#### 4.2 Verify Iops=3000 and State=in-use
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Iops:Iops,State:State}'
```
**Purpose:** Verify Iops=3000 and State=in-use

#### 4.3 Confirm the symptom is gone and the bottleneck has not moved to the…
**Type:** text
Over the next 10–15 minutes check: (1) alarm example-a-io2-queue-length returns to OK; (2) VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 0 and VolumeQueueLength < 1 for vol-0123456789abcdef0; (3) application write latency returns to baseline; (4) InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck for i-1234567890abcdef0_3 stay 0 and EBSByteBalance% does not drop. If the volume settles at ~3000 IOPS with VolumeIOPSExceededCheck=1 again, or the instance checks go to 1, the instance is now the limit; do not raise volume IOPS further.
**Purpose:** Confirm the symptom is gone and the bottleneck has not moved to the instance
**Advisory:** If more than ~3,000 IOPS is needed: move to c6i.2xlarge (12,000 IOPS, 298.0 MiB/s; needs stop/start in a maintenance window), or reduce throughput on gp3 co-tenant vol-1234567890abcdef0_18.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the saved configuration if the instance hits its EBS limit or…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000
```
**Purpose:** Restore the saved configuration if the instance hits its EBS limit or the cost is unacceptable
**Risks:** Brings back the original limit, high queue length and write latency., Uses another of the 4 modifications allowed per volume in a rolling 24h.
**Advisory:** Run only after the previous modification shows optimizing or completed.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Make the io2 volume's IOPS change permanent in your infrastructure code.
**Description:** Update the infrastructure definition (CloudFormation/CDK/Terraform) for vol-0123456789abcdef0 (Name tag example-a-io2) to Iops=3000 so the next deploy does not undo the manual change.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The infrastructure definition says Iops=3000, and a plan/diff against the live resource shows no IOPS change.
- A deploy does not trigger a ModifyVolume back to 1000 IOPS.

#### 2. Size storage against the instance EBS baseline and spot saturation earlier.
**Description:** Add CloudWatch alarms on VolumeIOPSExceededCheck for vol-0123456789abcdef0, and on InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck, InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and EBSByteBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_3. Document that total EBS demand on this instance must stay under 149.0 MiB/s and 6,000 IOPS.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The alarms exist and fire when a volume or the instance hits its EBS limit.
- The sizing rule (total of all volumes ≤ instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS) is documented next to the infrastructure code.

{"id": "3ae14017-a080-46b5-a424-1b5d5dcbef33", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "IMPORTANT: Respond entirely in English (observations, findings, summaries). Technical terms, resource names, and ARNs stay in their original form.

Incident: CloudWatch alarm [redacted ARN] (VolumeQueueLength avg > 1.0, 3 of 3 one-minute datapoints) went to ALARM at 2026-11-23T16:23:04Z. Application write latency is up. AWS account 012345678901_1, us-east-1 (use1-az4 / us-east-1a).

Established root cause (verified, treat as ground truth). Mitigation category: Limits (volume provisioned IOPS).
- Volume [redacted ARN] io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge, Nitro) as /dev/sdf.
- From 16:20 to 16:48 UTC it is pinned at 999.7–1000.3 IOPS (100% writes, 8 KiB per I/O, about 7.81 MiB/s). VolumeIdleTime is about 0%, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck=1 every 5 minutes from 16:15, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck=0, queue length about 1.33, write latency about 1.33 ms/op. Before 16:19 the volume was 100% idle.
- Volume status is ok, VolumeStalledIOCheck=0, there are no open AWS Health EBS/EC2 events, and this volume has no ModifyVolume record (DescribeVolumesModifications and CloudTrail for the last 24h are both empty). Running FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (aws:ebs:volume-io-latency) targets a different volume, vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which is not attached to this instance. Not an impairment.
- Instance layer: the c6i.xlarge EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (= 149.0 MiB/s); the maximum is 40,000 IOPS and 1,250 MB/s. Summed demand of all 4 attached volumes is about 1,502 IOPS and about 132.9 MiB/s (EC2 EBSRead+WriteBytes). EBSIOBalance%/EBSByteBalance% = 99%, and InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck/InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck = 0. The instance is not binding now.
- Co-tenant: gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 (20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s) runs flat at about 125.07 MiB/s / 500 IOPS (its own throughput limit, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck=1). It uses most of the instance throughput baseline. The root volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_19 runs at about 0.02 MiB/s and gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 is idle.

Sizing constraint: instance throughput headroom = 149.0 − 125.07 − 0.02 ≈ 23.9 MiB/s. At 8 KiB I/O that allows about 3,060 IOPS on the io2 volume before the summed demand reaches the instance EBS baseline. io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS/GiB, so 10 GiB caps at 10,000 IOPS. Candidate change: ModifyVolume vol-0123456789abcdef0 Iops 1000 -> 3000 (online). The true application demand is unknown because the cap masks it. If more than about 3,000 IOPS is needed, the instance becomes the limit. Then the option is an instance type change, for example c6i.2xlarge (baseline 12,000 IOPS, 312.5 MB/s = 298.0 MiB/s), or lowering the gp3 co-tenant's throughput usage. Elastic Volumes rule: up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24h. No deployment or commit is involved.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "be4cf6a1-88d3-4b6f-a953-22db9ffa621b", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_rMBiVUPnCMR266ijlo7nGB", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: storage-ebs-expertise
     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
